ALBUM
REVIEWS
CHRISTINE PLAYS
IT HOT—Score
Here’s a prime opportunity for all piano-organ
lovers
to hear
a happy,
infectious
style on
the
keyboard. A
veteran
of
the
night
club
circuit,
Christine makes her wax debut with a bevy
of
favorites. The piano speaks lively on “El Cuman-
chero” and the organ keeps up the handclapping
feeling on “Twelfth Street Rag.” Album is loaded
with programmable material, so watch it for air-
play.
JAZZ PICKS
A LOVE SUPREME—John
Coltrane—Impulse!
A-77
“This album
is a humble
offering to Him. An
attempt
to
say
‘Thank
you
God.’ ”
Thus
John
Coltrane describes his four-part set. As a tribute,
a religious expression, and a magnificent work of
soulful music, the
set
is
a tremendous
achieve-
ment.
The
saxist,
and
his
crew, McCoy Tyner
(piano), Jimmy Garrison
(bass) and Elvin Jones
(drums) turn in a great performance. The compo-
sition itself builds to a superb climax in “Psalm”
after
beautifully
developing
through
the
first
three
sections. An
exquisite
set.
TO SWEDEN WITH LOVE—Art Farmer Quar-
tet—Atlantic 1430
The
Art
P’armer
Quartet
use
six
traditional
Swedish folk songs as the basis for their interest-
ing jazz improvisations. Most of the tracks retain
some
of the melancholy
so prevalent in Scandi-
navian music, but the ebulant Farmer on flugel-
horn, and Jim Hall’s guitar add zest to the
ses-
sion. Steve Swallow, the bassist, has a fine solo on
“De
Salde
Sina Hemman,”
and drummer
Pete
LaRoca plays well in support throughout. Other
tunes include: “Visa Vid Midsommartid,” and “Va
Da Du?” One of the best outings that Farmer has
cut in quite a while.
JAZZ BEST BETS
JAZZ FROM
RUSSIA—Golstan-Nosov
Quintet
and the Yusef Wainstain Orchestra—Vee Jay 2504
The opening of
this album was
culled from a
track
in
Miles
Davis’
“Sketches
in
Spain,” but
past the first refrain the jazz is new and exciting-
ly different. The crews cutting the session are all
Rusian, and well worth noting for their ability to
compose
(all
seven
selections
are
originals)
as
well as swing. The talents of Constantin Nosov on
trumpet
and
Gennadi
Golstain on
alto
sax
are
considerable
as they groove on tracks
like “La-
ment,” “Rosinant
in
Andalusia,” and the
Soviet
march tune “Polyushko-Polye.”
LIFE TIME—Anthony William^Blue Note 4180
This album, over a year in preparation, features
five works by drummers Anthony Williams, who
headed
the combo
in
the
session.
These
funky
works have a special quality of working their way
inside the listener and
exciting his conscious re-
action to the sounds. The infectious tracks “To-
morrow Afternoon” and “Two Pieces of One (Red
and Green)” are expertly executed examples
of
this. The group of Herbie Hancock on piano, Sam
Rivers
on
tenor
sax, and
several
other
equally
fine musicians. An attractive
set.
CLASSICAL PICKS
THE ROMANTIC STRINGS OF ANDRE KOS-
TELANETZ—Columbia ML 6111/MS 6711
Although this release
is included in Columbia’s
classical line, it features selections which will ap-
peal to many buyers shopping for popular disks.
The tunes are of such board appeal that only the
renditions
tab
them
connoisseur’s
fare.
Tender
music for romantic listening
is the key feature,
and
the
tracks:
“Londonderry
Air,”
“Green-
sleeves,”
and
“Ave
Maria”
(both
the
Bach-
Gounod,
and
Schubert
versions)
are
superior
samples in this mood.
RAVEL MA MERE L’OYE, LA VALSE,
BO-
LERO;
Pierre
Monteux
conducting
the
London
Symphony Orchestra; Philips PHM 500-059/PHS
900-059
The lush sound of Maurice Ravel’s impression-
ist strains
is presented here
in
its
three forms,
the
soft,
exotic “Ma Mere
L’Oye;
the
foi'ceful,
vibrant
“Bolero,”
and
the
middle
phase,
“La
Valse,” which
is somewhere between the two
in
volume and tempo.
Splendid readings by
Pierre
Monteux,
at the head
of the London Symphony
Orchestra,
are
given
to each
of the works, and
they come off superbly. The popular compositions
make a wonderful selection in the Philips catalog.
A
fine
addition, which would complement many
classical
collections.

Seeburg Discotheque Team Covers 7,000 Miles To Date
CHICAGO—Stanley Jarocki, national
promotion manager
for
the
Seeburg
Corporation, is concentrating through-
out the United States, along with Jo-
seph
Panarinfo,
the
originator
in
France
of Discotheque, and a consul-
tant
for
Seeburg
in
assisting music
operators
in
establishing discotheque
locations in appropriate places. Actu-
ally, Jarocki
is usually headed in one
direction while Arnold Silverman, his
counterpart
in
the
Seeburg
Disco-
theque plan, is headed in the opposite
direction.
“When Joseph
decided
to come
to
the United States as an exclusive con-
sultant to Seeburg, he had no idea of
the
size of the United
States nor
of
the
vast
difference
in
temperature,”
Jarocki
said. In just a one week
pe-
riod,
Jarocki and Panarinfo
traveled
In Chickashaw, Oklahoma:

right:

Blankenbeckler,
Seeburg’s
regional
vice

Joseph Pan-
arinfo,
Ruby
Williams,
discotheque
dance
instructress;
J.
C.
Hunter,
owner and manager of El Rancho, in
Chickashaw;
and
Stan
Jarocki.
over 7,000 miles by air and 800 miles
by
car,
visiting Albuquerque, N.
M.,
El Paso, Beaumont, Turtle Bayou and
Houston,
Texas;
Philadelphia,
Pa.
and
Whitesboro, New
York.
Jarocki further revealed that, “from
the balmy weather of the Southwest,
he ran into a raging blizzard near Wa-
tertown, New York after helping
in-
augurate Discotheque dancing
at the
Blue Note a Go-Go, Whitesboro, New
York for owner, Chet Rey, and opera-
tor, A1
Misiaszek, Paramount Music,
Utica, New York, but despite the bliz-
zard,
the
installations
came
off
on
schedule.”
Jarocki
and
Panarinfo
were assisted part of the way by See-
burg’s regional vice president Richard
Murphy.
The photos shown above
(left and
right) depict some of the action which
took place opening night of the disco-
theque
entertainment
in
Philadel-
phia’s RDA Club, where the Seeburg
package
was
installed
by

NEW YORK—Ampex

officials

a

of

new

machine
industry.

refused to amplify this comment. The
model uses a %-inch tape and records
at a high speed—100 inches per

location

Comic
Kirby Inked
As Chess Chanter
NEW YORK—Leonard Chess, head of
Chess
Records,
has
announced
the
sigrning of an exclusive recording con-
tract
between
his
firm
and
mimic-
comedian George Kirby. The deal was
negotiated
in
Chicago, where
Kirby
was appearing at Mr.
Kelly’s, by his
manager Charles Carpenter. The un-
usual part of the deal is that the pact
calls for Kirby
to
cut
as a
vocalist,
with his
first single release presently
in the works and release of his initial
effort
scheduled
for an
early March
release. The tunes
selected are from
the Anthony Newley show “The Roar
of the
Greasepaint.”
Kirby
attracted
interest
to
his
singing
ability during
the past year
in nightclubs, at fairs and on top TV
shows. Numerous offers came
in bid-
ding for his comedy talent; however,
Kirby was of the opinion the market
had been saturated by comedy albums
and
that
a
broader
audience
could
be reached by recording as a vocalist.
Chess
shared
his
belief
and
signed
him.
Following
his engagement
at
Mr.
Kelly’s,
the
comedian
will
headline
for two weeks
at the Copacabana
in
New York, beginning March 25; per-
form

$1
Million Musical Near?
NEW YORK—The day of the $1 mil-
lion Broadway
musical may
not
be
far off.
Just
last
season,
it
was
possible
to
mount
an
expensive
show
for
around
$400,000.
But, doing a
lavish
show
this
year
is
running
at
least
$600,000.
' “Baker
Street,” which opened
last
week,
has
been
officially
tagged
at
costing
$610,000. A few weeks
ago,
“Kelly” proved a $650,000 fiasco.

season,
a budget of
$600,000
has
been
established—it’ll
probably
cost
more—^for

new
Alan
Jay
Lerner-Burton Lane
Musical, “On A

Can
See
Forever.”
NBC
is

for

is

$60,000. RCA
Victor
Rec-
ords,

the

cast LP.

LIVE FROM LEDBETTER’S—The Back
Porch
Majority—Epic LN24134/BN26134
Randy Spark’s lively, rollickin’ Back Porch Ma-
jority belts out a collection of toe-tappers
in
its
latest package, recorded live at Ledbetter’s in Los
Angeles. The group strays from the path of the
well-worn folk standards with driving renditions
of new folk-styled
tunes, “Walk The Road” and
“Where Will You Be?,” plus the comedy
tunes,
“Out
Behind
The
Barn,”
“Oedipus
Rex”
and
“Smash
Flops.”
Folk
bulfs
should
really
enjoy
this package.
ROCKIN’ FOLK — Brian Hyland — Philips PHM
200-158/PHS 600-158
Rock and roll star Brian Hyland has turned his
attention
to the
folk
field
in
this
outing, which
matches the best selections of the latter with the
soft rock
style and guitar talents
of the
singer,
and comes
out
a
lovely
listening
set.
Hyland’s
voice is in good form as he puts down songs like
“Slowin’ In The Wind,” “Silver Threads And Gol-
den Needles” and “Where Have All The Flowers
Gone.” The set should see a fine reaction among
the singer’s many fans, and folksters looking for
a new sound.
1965 SAN REMO FESTIVAL — 12 WINNING
SONGS—Various
Artists—London
International
TW 91372/SW 99372
Each year, the choicest selections in the Italian
musical repertoire are selected for the world fam-
ous San Remo Festival; London International has
culled the top 12 for this platter, recorded in Italy
by C.G.D. The selections are the tunes that were
elected
to the
final
competition, and include the
winning “Se Piangi, Se Ridi,” and runner-ups “Le
Colline
Sono
In
Fiore,” and
“lo Che Non Vivo
Senza Te,” among others. This
is a
fine set that
should see fine reaction due to the wide coverage
of
the
event,
and
the
spectacular
cover
photo,
as well as very good performances.
NANCY AMES—Liberty LRP 3400/LST
7400
Nancy
Ames,
whose
previous
repertory was
culled from
folk
sturdies,
changes
her
pace
on
this album and comes up with a fine package of
pop
ballads. The
thrush
handles
torch numbers
with the same throaty feeling and powerful style
that
has made
her
a
regular
feature
of
TV’s
“This Was The Week That Was.” The LP includes
“Let It Be Me” and “Because Of You” and prom-
ises to receive strong attention.
MANY A MILE—Buffy Sainte-Marie—Vanguard
VRS-9171/VSD-79171
Vanguard Records has made many
strides
in
expanding the folk
field by uncovering less com-
mercialized
singers who have become leaders
in
the
ethnic music world. One
of the most recent
of these
discoveries, Buffy Sainte-Marie, created
a stir with her initial LP, and this second outing,
“Many A
Mile,”
retains
the freshness and
sim-
plicity which has gained her a devoted following.
Among the fine tunes found here are: “Los Pes-
cadores,” “Johnny Be
Fair,” and “Come
All Ye
Fair and Tender
Girls.”
Fine
vocal and
instru-
mental talent well displayed.
DICK WILLIAMS’ KIDS SING FOR BIG PEO-
PLE (AND LITTLE PEOPLE, TOO)—Argo 4041
Argo
Records
has come up
with
a
novel
set
which should garner lots of air time by virtue of
the change-of-pace this package provides, and the
unique
idea behind
a
sextet aged
8-11
doing a
bunch of evergreens. The album has all the fresh-
ness of Patience and Prudence polished a bit, but
still maintains the youthful flavor which gives a
new
slant
to
tunes
like
“All Of Me,”
“It’s The
Talk Of The Town,” and “Come Rain Or Come
Shine.” Fine orking by Dick Williams gives
the
set added appeal. Could break wide open.
FAVORITE GOSPELS—The Gospel Clouds of Joy
—Nashboro 7023
The Gospel Clouds of Joy should attract quite
a bit of attention among gospel-blues lovers with
their latest package of soulful offerings served up
with
a
steady
beat
and
loads
of
feeling.
The
crew comes up with exciting versions of “Get My
Crown,” and “Laid My Burdens Down” and deep-
ly moving laments in “Don’t Know Without The
Lord,” and “Give God A
Chance.” A
lively
set,
with
well
done
organ
accompaniment, and very
fine vocal work.
’S MAKE IT—Art Blakey and the Jazz Messen-
gers—Limelight LM 82001/LS 82001
The newest Art Blakey disk to
hit the market
has more
potential
than most
of
his
previous
efforts
for
two
very
good
reasons.
First,
the
crew works up a set that is as musically appeal-
ing
as
any
they
have
done
before;
Blakey
is
magnificent,
Lee Morgan
(trumpet)
and
Curtis
Fuller (trombone)
are
in top form together and
on
solos; John Gilmore,
(tenor sax), John Hicks
(piano) and Vic Sproles
(bass)
also turn in fine
workmanship. Added sales appeal
is in the Lime-
light packaging, which should
sell some tyros on
the album by the informative data on the
cuts,
and bios included between the double-fold cover.
Tracks feature: “Faith,” “Little Hughie,” and the
title tune “ ’S Make It.”
I’M TRYIN’ TO GET HOME—Donald Byrd-
Blue Note 4188
Here’s an imaginative jazz package
spotlight-
ing ace trumpeter Donald Byrd
(he
also plays
flugelhorn
on
the
set)
backed by
a
full
brass
section
and
an
eight-voice
chorus.
Although
crackling solos do exist herein, the chorus is effec-
tively utilized as an
attractive, cohesive compli-
ment
to
the
varied
midstream
progressions.
Among the highlights here are: “Brother Isaac,”
“Noah” and “Pearly Gates.”
JAZZ BEST BETS
THE KING AND
I—The Mastersounds—World-
Pacific 1831
Rodgers and Hammerstein’s
score from “The
King and I”
is taken for a soft groovy ride by a
fine sounding quartet, the Mastersounds, yet the
tunes
are
all
respectfully
treated
in
this most

set-up
and
modulates
between
their
easy
quiet
sound on the ballads like “My Lord and Master,”
and “We Kiss
in
the
Shadows,” and
a moving
catchy up-beat on
cuts
like
“Shall We Dance.”
This
set
is very well
suited
to most mid-stream
tastes, and could see some pop
sales reaction as
well.
THE BLUES—Lightning
Hopkins—Mainstream
56040/S/6040
Mainstream has helped fatten its catalog much
to the delight of blues fanciers by making avail-
able a number of tracks that were once collector’s
items, and this release of sides cut in 1950-51 by
Lightning
Hopkins,
should
see
a
fine
reaction
among
connoisseurs
of
the
down-home,
earthy
blues music. The renditions are simple and poig-
nant, the guitar accompaniment is excellent, and
the
tunes
themselves
are
brilliant. Among
the
songs done are
“Hello
Central,” “Gotta Move,”
and “Everything Happens to Me.”

PAGNINI: CONCERTO NO. 2 IN B MINOR, OP.

The Italianata second violin concerto of Paga-

is a rarely recorded opus which

SOMEBODY
LOVES ME—Perry Como—RCA
Camden CAL 858/CAS 858
In
the
traditionally
smooth Como
style,
the
chanter
glides
through
a
series
of
nostalgic
numbers on this LP offering. With the able back-
ing of the Mitchell Ayres ork and the Ray Charles
singers,
the
crooner
once
again
spins
a magic
web
of wax. The track includes
such
old-timers
as “The Island of Forgotten Lovers” and “That
Old Gang
of
Mine.”
Looks
like
another Como
success.
THE NEW DANCE SOUND OF BILLY BUT-
TERFIELD—Joy JL 1003
Billy
Butterfield
and
his
ork
cash-in
on
the
discotheque trend with this hard-driving program
of
chestnuts
dished-up
in
an
appealing
terpsi-
chorean-oriented fashion. The big band combines
elements of blues and Dixieland
into
a
slick
co-
hesive
musical
fusion. Among
the
best
dancin’
bets here are “Big Noise From Winnetka,” “My
Johnny
Is
Coming
Home,”
and
“Ballin’
The
Jack.”
JAZZ PICKS
OUT OF THE WOODS—The
George
Shearing
Quintet—Capitol T/ST 2272
Composer Gary Burton has created a nice
col-
lection
of
swingers
for waxing by
the
George
Shearing Quintet and the Four Woodwinds. The
jazzmen’s lively session
is topped
off with some
exciting numbers
including “The
Great Fugue”
which has an interesting second session with two
independent four-part fugues, and “Dialogue For
Two Pianos” with some fine dual improvisation on
the ivories and a good bit of keyboard soloing by
Shearing.
ELLA AT JUAN-LES PINS—Ella Fitzgerald—
Verve V/V6-4065
The international jazz festival at Juan-les Pins
provides the background for a dandy package of
Ella
Fitzgerald
grooves.
Since
there
were
no
plans to record the concert the thrush’s warblings
were waxed from
a video
tape. The always im-
pressive
artist
highlights
the
LP
with
such
memoz’able
tunes
as
“I’ve
Got You Under My
Skin” and “The Lady
is a Tramp” plus her im-
provisational “The Cricket Song.”
HEDY WEST
VOL. 2—Vanguard VRS
9162/
VSD 79162
Hedy West has come out with another fine col-
lection of folk tunes from her large repertory on
this new Vanguard album. Her style is traditional
and her approach
is
eclectic. She has the
ability
to make the
audience
“feel”
or
“live” the
song
without
using
the
pop-styled
sounds
and
gim-
micks
of
the modern
folk-stylists.
The LP
in-
cludes
the
mountain
sound
of
“Moonshiner’s
Lament” and the tender, “Poor Little Lost Baby.”

membered today, others known but to pop music

Crosby

ings,

covers

in words and photos. A gold-mine
of talent and

NEW YORK—The discotheque sound

vorite

of

Joe.
The
first

is also releasing a single
from

issue.

ery
will

material
from

material

that

rnan
for Rowe
juke-boxes
that
spe-
cialize
in the discotheque
sound.
Atlantic
should
greatly
benefit
from
feature
articles
in many
na-
tional magazines that have noted the
discotheque fad with strong mentions
of Killer Joe.

Honors Tucker
NEW YORK—Vet

Tucker was

na,

Catron
Concludes
European
Deals
NEW YORK — South Mountain Mu-
sic’s
general
professional
manager
Stan Catron has
just returned from
a ten-day European business
tour.
While in Italy, Catron acquired the
rights
for
the
Italian
flick “A
Fist
Full Of Dollars” (“Un Pugne Di Dol-
lar!”), which
is
due
to
open
in
the
U.S.
later
this
year, and assigned a
writer
to
pen
English
lyrics
to
the
film’s
main
theme.
He
also
placed
five of the pubbery’s songs with CGD
Records A&R chief, Giuseppi Gianini,
for future waxings.
On
the
French
scene,
pacts
were
set up
to record “Won’t You Be My
Girl,” which was done
in the
States
by
Tommy
Sands
last
year,
and
“Don’t
Go
’Way”
to
be
waxed
by
Sylvia
Vartin.
There were
also
con-
ferences
in
Paris
with
Michel
Le-
grand,
composer
of
the
score
for
Academy
Award
nominee
“Umbrel-
las Of Cherbourg.” The pubbery han-
dles the score in the U.S.
Activities
in England included
set-
ting up
recordings
of
South
Moun-
tain tunes by
British
artists, among
whom
are
Billy
Fury
and
Lonny
Donnegan.
Catron, who also opened branch of-
fices for the firm in Rome and Paris
will be spending the next few weeks
pushing
“I

Stop
Thinking
Of
You,” by Bobby Martin, and “You’re
Breaking My
Heart,” by

Block-
busters, both

Al Ham Heads Music Depf.,
Label of Electronovision
NEW YORK—Al Ham has been ap-
pointed
vice
president
in
charge
of
all
musical
activities
for
Electrono-
vision
and
president
of
Electrono-
vision Records it was announced last
week
by
Bill
Sargent,
president
of
the
company.
Electronovision
is
the
new, speedy feature
film process.
Ham
will
continue
to operate
out
of New York. He recently completed
the music for the company’s upcom-
ing production of “Harlow.”
He had previously been
associated
with Joy Records as a producer,
ar-
ranger
and
conductor
and
was
at
Columbia Records as a producer and
associate director of Pop A&R under
Mitch
Miller.
The
soundtrack
for
Electronoyision’s
“Harlow,”
which
will
be
a
presentation
of
Marshall
Naify and
Bill Sargent and released
by Magna Distribution Corp., will be
“laid
in” during
actual filming on a
motion picture sound stage for what
is
believed
to
be
the
first
time
in
picture history. Theatrofilm will star
Dorothy Provine in the title role from
a screenplay by Karl Tunberg.
Album of the score will be released
by Electronovision Records
in
April.

WB Inks Three: Jobim,
Smith And Lightfoot
BURBANK—Antonio
Carlos
Jobim,
one of the leading composers of bossa
nova
material, has been
signed
to a
recording contract with Warner Bro-
thers
Records.
The
pact
will
cover
Jobim as a recording
artist, both
as
a
soloist
and
orchestral
accompani-
ment for other artists on the WB-Re-
prise roster. Negotiations were carried
out by Mike Maitland. Maitland also
announced
the
signing
to
exclusive
recording
contracts
of
pianist
Paul
Smith
and
singer-composer
Gordon
Lightfoot.
Jobim came into prominence in the
United States through his many South
American compositions, most notably
“One Note
Samba,” “The
Girl from
Ipanema,” “Desifinado,” and “Medita-
tion.”
Several
recent
best-selling
al-
bums have come from Jobim’s compo-
sitions,
including
“Getz-Gilberto.”
Currently
residing
in
Hollywood,
Jobim
is
collaborating
with
lyricist
Ray
Gilbert, who
is
also
acting
as
Jobim’s publishing representative and
manager. Together, they are nearing
completion
of
contract
negotiations
for two
film
scoring
projects. Jobim
plans
to remain
in the
U.S.
for an-
other six months before returning to
Brazil, at which time he will arrange
for his future recording and compos-
ing
activities
both
in
the
U.S.
and
South America.
Lightfoot,
a
Toronto
resident,
is
composer
of the
current
Peter, Paul
and Mary
single,
“For
Lovin’
Me.”
Discovered by the trio, Lightfoot was
signed to the album and single record-
ing pact by Joe Smith, head of singles
A & R for the label.
Srnith, one
of Hollywood’s
leading
studio
musicians,
has
already
been
slated by
Warners’ Jimmy
Hilliard,
who
will be recording Smith, for an
album
release
in
April. The
pianist,
a featured performer on many albums
recorded
in
Hollywood,
will
be
re-
corded in
live concert performance.

HOLLYWOOD—Los
Angeles
radio
is
now
experiencing
its
greatest
transition in recent history with even
more
switches
expected
during
the
next few weeks. Several deejays have
returned here from
such widespread
areas as New York, Chicago, Phoenix
and
San
Francisco and
others
have
simply packed
their record bags and
moved from one
local
station
to
an-
other.
Reb
Foster,
for
example,
left
KRLA
in
mid-week
and was
heard
the following night on arch rival sta-
tion KFWB.
Joe Yocam and
Roger
Christian
have
already
left KFWB
to make room for Foster and for the
return of B. Mitch Reed, back again
after two years with WMCA in New
York.
Bill Ballance has moved up
to
the mid-moming
slot
at KFWB and
Reed
will be heard once again from
6-9 P.M.
Jim Randolf, after a four year ab-
sence, has returned
to L.A. and can
be heard again on KGFJ. Rudy Har-
vey
has
switched
from
KGFJ
to
KDAY and Dick Biondi, back in town,
is once again on KRLA.
KBLA, which recently increased
its
signal, now has Tom Clay, last heard
on KDAY and Dick Whittington, pre-
viously heard here on KLAC, has the
3-7 P.M.
spot on KGIL.
Roscoe,
last
heard on KGFJ, and “Huggie Boy”
have
also
been
added
to
KBLA’s
staff.
At KHJ there are plans to switch
the musical format from
“talk”,
al-
bums
and
jazz
to
a
contemporary
“formula” sound and
already KHJ’s
news department has been informed
that
“in depth” news
reporting
will
be cut back to
five minutes. Michael
Jackson
has
already
left
and
Mai
Alberts’ 15 minute sportscast has been
dropped.
It
is reliably reported
that
Sam
Riddle
will be
leaving KFWB
and
will
join KHJ’s revamped
staff
and
that
several
other
local
jocks
will translocate within
the next few
weeks.
KFI,
the
local NBC
affiliate,
has
just announced
that
Geoff Edwards,
former
P.D.
at KHJ,
will
soon
be
heard mornings from 6-10.
At KNX, the CBS outlet, the music
policy for weekends has changed radi-
cally and now many Top 40 hits are
aired in place of the Sunday morning
show which
had
featured
the
Mor-
mon Tabernacle
Choir.

Plant

MUSIC TO SOOTHE THAT TIGER—Herbert
Rehbein—Decca DL
4584/DL
74584
European
export Herbert Rehbein
guides
his
lush
ork
in
a
rich-sounding
tour
of
“cheek-to-
cheek” music with
this
outing, recorded
in Eu-
rope. The
orkster, who
also does arranging for
Bert
Kaempfert,
has
compiled
a
fine
batch
of
vintage love songs mixed
in with
a few compo-
sitions
that
he
co-penned
with
Kaempfert and
has waxed a beautiful package of romance-filled
nostalgia.
The
LP
features
Emil
Wurster
on
tenor
sax and
is highlighted by
such haunting
oldies
as
“Chances Are”
and “Speak
Low.”
HARD TRAVELIN’—Woody
Guthrie—Disc
D-
llO/DS-1110
Woody Guthrie, who is reputed to have written
over
a
thousand
folk
ballads,
has
collected
a
dozen
of
his
self-penned
tunes and waxed
an-
other fine platter. The balladeer’s simple and un-
cluttered deliverance of his mountain-styled mu-
sic
is
enhanced
throughout
the
album
by
the
able
backing
of
Cisco
Houston,
and,
at
times.
Sonny
Terry.
Some
of
the
more
well-known
Guthrie tunes included in the package are “Chis-
holm
Trail” and “Hard
Travelin’.”
ADVENTURES
IN FLAMENCO—Carlos
Mon-
toya—ABC
Paramount
ABC/ABCS-508
The fiery flavor of Spain rings out in the spec-
tacular performance
of
Carlos Montoya
on
his
latest ABC
Paramount
album,
“Adventures
In
Flamenco.” The
intricate and
exquisite mastery
which
Montoya
has

in

previous
LP’s shines in this one, despite the fact that this
work
was
recorded
from
unrehearsed
unprp-
grammed
material. The
guitarist’s
fans,
lovers
of flamenco music, and flocks of folkists who are
fascinated by virtuoso guitar talents should turn
out
in force
for
this
item.
Included among
the
eight

are:
“Albaicin
Fla-
menco,”
“Ritmos

and
“Toque
Murci-
ano.”

&

74619
Two young stars of the TV package, “The Vir-

of the pack-
age

TROPICAL MADNESS — Los
Wawanco — Decca
DL 4565/DL 74565
The authentic Latin sound has been captured on
this Decca album recorded
in Argentina by Los
Wawanco. The group’s debut in the United States
should be a good one, since their excellent musi-
cal offering ought to find a ready market among
lovers of the Latin beat, and dancing. The act is
terpsichoreally tops with rhythms like the stand-
by cha-cha and merengue
shuffled with cumbias
and guarachas. Included on the
bill-of-fare
are:
“Cambia de Colombia,” “El Pescador” and “Deja
Que Suba La Marea.” Vocals add to the listening
enjoyment.

The

Fine

—Columbia CL 2292/CS 9092
Bud

ing both for admirers of Powell and Monk fans,

THE INCOMPARABLE BOLA SETE—Fantasy
3364/8364
Bola
Sete
has

one

artist on the mod-
ern

due

This

Drifting

525
The talented James Moody displays his virtu-

in

The

be showing around

and
artists.

Columbia
Pictures
Makes
Fiscal Gains
NEW YORK —
Columbia
Pictures
Corporation,
the parent company
of
Colpix Records, has issued
its report
for the
first
six months
of the
1965
fiscal
year, showing a gain over the
corresponding period of the previous
year.
The gross income for the new pe-
riod was quoted at $3,034,000, before
taxes, with
an
estimated
$1,390,000,
after
taxes,
or
74^
earnings
per
share of common stock. This
is com-
pared to the previous year’s gross of
$2,659,000 which showed, after taxes,
earnings
of
$1,096,000,
or
574
per
share.
Meanwhile,
the
company’s
subsid-
iary,
Screen Gems, has
already
sold
four network programs and has
re-
newed five of the six series presently
on the networks, for the largest num-
ber of packages that they have ever
presented on the networks in any one
year.

“Broken-

ing Time” by Elena. On the LP front,

C-P Sustained Loss
In '64
NEW YORK—Bernie
Lowe,
presi-
dent of Cameo-Parkway Records, has
reported that the
1964 operations of
the corporation, after taxes, resulted
in a loss of $499,319, or 83
a share,
compared
to a
profit of $655,498, or
$1.10 per share
in
1963.
Lowe noted that the loss could be
attributed
to two main
factors:
the
lack
of
a
big
singles
hit
and
the
“unprecedented” number of disks re-
turned
for
credit by
the
label’s
dis-
tribs.
Looking
ahead,
Lowe
stated
that
the company had expanded
its
offices
in New
York
for
the
discovery
of
new
talent. “We
will
continue
our
efforts
in
Philadelphia, which
in the
past has been a most fertile field for
talent and which we expect will
con-
tinue to furnish us with bright new
stars,”
the
exec
said.
Lowe further stated that the com-
pany’s new budget line, Wyncote, had
opened
up
distribution
areas
where
the company had not been
selling in
the past.
“We are confident,” he
said, “that
current
savings
in
operations
initi-
ated by our general manager, Harry
Silverstein,
together
with
profits
from our Silver Plastics division and
our Wyncote budget album
line
will
result
in
a
profitable
year,
even
if
we
fail to produce a single
‘hit’
rec-
ord.” Concluded Lowe:
“.
.
.
the
fi-
nancial condition of our company re-
mains
strone.”
Richard Hayman's Death
Is "Highly
Exaggerated"
NEW YORK—Richard Hayman, the
arranger-harmonica
player,
is
very
much
alive. Rumors had been
circu-
lating
around
the
trade
last
week
that the music man had
died. Hay-
man
quoted
to
Cash
Box
^ Mark
Twain’s classic line following his sup-
posed demise: “Rumors of my death
are
highly
exaggerated.”
Harry James
Inks
Pact With
Dot
HOLLYWOOD—Dot
Records
prexy
Randy Wood last week announced the
signing
of
world
famous
trumpet
player-bandleader Harry James
to
a
recording contract. The terms require
James and his band to record a mini-
mum
of
three Dot albums per year
and one per annum for the diskery’s
subsidiary banner, Hamilton Records.
Tom Mack, label veep, flew to Har-
rah’s Tahoe for meetings with Harry
James to plan the recording schedule.
According to Mack, the
initial album
will be recorded in a Las Vegas studio
during
James’
forthcoming
engage-
ment at the Flamingo Hotel
in that
city. Currently working to clear time
for these sessions is Pee Wee Monte,
the artist’s personal manager.

Tangerine Records
Moves To New RPM Building
LOS ANGELES—Tangerine
Records,
owned by ABC Paramount recording
artist Ray
Charles, has moved from
its New York
offices
to
the
newly-
opened RPM International Building in
Los Angeles, also owned and operated
by Charles.
The
label,
which
will
continue
to
be
distributed
by
ABC-Paramount,
lists among
its
artists, Louis Jordan,
Percy
Mayfield, Margie Hendrix and
Lula
Reed,
as
well
as
newcomers
Shirley Gunter, Terrell Prude, George
Wydell, Marvin Jenkins, Barbara Mid-
dleton, Donnie McGowan, the Vocals,
the
Shockers,
the
Vala-Quons
and
Larry and Darryl Perrault.
Mike
Akopoff,
formerly
with
Dot
and Buckeye, and associated with the
production
of
twelve
million-dollar
record
sellers,
has
been
named
as
A&R man, and former music teacher
Otis Hayes
will
be
the
label’s
staff
arranger. Others on the
staff include
Micki McMillan, former executive sec-
retary
at Hollywood’s
Screen Actors
Guild, who will take care of adminis-
tration, and Jan
Conn, who had her
own public relations firm in the mid-
west,
directing
public
relations.
The multi-talented Charles also has
five more
of
his corporations housed
in
his
new
building,
including
Ray
Charles
Enterprises,
Inc.,
Tangerine
Music
Publishing
Corp., Racer Music
Publishing
Corp.,
Racer
Personal
Mgmt.
Corp., and
R.
P. M.
Interna-
tional,
Inc.
An open house
is being planned for
early this spring and the date will be
announced upon completion of the ar-
rangements.

######## cb 1965-04-10 p34  [blue\s+note]
ALBUM REVIEWS
THE
VI VELASCO ALBUM — VeeJay
VJLP/
VJS 1135
Following’
up
her
recent
singles
noisemaker,
“You Are My Sunshine,” Vi Velasco has
finally
made
her
debut
in
the album
department. The
petite songstress, who drew a lot of attention in
her Broadway
stints with “Flower Drum Song”
and “No
Strings,” makes an impressive
bid for
further attention with this LP as she dishes out
a
delightful display of
ditties. Some
of the top
tracks include “Never Less Than Yesterday” and
“If You Must Break A Heart,” as well as both
sides of the aforementioned single
outing.
RARE!
HOT! & COLE PORTER—Sheila
M.
Sanders—Philips PHM 200-169 /PHS 600-169
The evergreen catalog of the
late Cole Porter
is put
aside
here
in favor
of
his more
obscure
numbers,
all
of which were fashioned with
the
same polish he employed on his
hits, but with a
far greater dash of wryness. They are performed
by
stylist Sheila Sanders with updated, jazz-feel
good-nature,
even
the
dated
tear-jerker,
“Hot
House Rose.” Phil Moore arranged (and conducts)
the hip
settings. These performances
are bound
to get more exposure than a straight, theatrical
approach to these “in” songs.
THE STATE FUNERAL OF
SIR WINSTON
CHURCHILL—United Artists 3427
The many people who purchased memorial
al-
bums
issued
at the
death
of Winston
Churchill
will
also want
this
recording
of
the
complete
state funeral ceremony as reported by the Brit-
ish Broadcasting Corporation. Richard Dimpleby
narrates and comments upon the action which in-
cludes the march through London to the cemetery,
and
includes
speeches by many
officials,
salutes
and hymns. The coverage of this memorable event
is complete and a stirring moment of history
is
here beautifully captured.
PETER BRADY, AN EXCITING NEW VOICE
ON THE MOVE—Capitol T/ST 2286
A new face on the horizon, Peter Brady makes
a memorable debut into the album field with this
initial Capitol package. The
artist, who can put
a
song
across
without
echo
chambers
or
gim-
micks, displays a multi-faceted talent as he glides
through tender ballads, backed by the lush string
arrangements of Marty Paich, then explodes with
his stimulating renditions of solid swing numbers
with Shorty Rogers
brass. Top tracks here are
the
kick-off
romancer, “Who
Are
We?,”
and
finger-popper “Something Happens To Me.”
MY HUSBAND AND I—Eleanor
Roosevelt—
Columbia 02L-314
Eleanor
Roosevelt
recalls many
of the major
incidents and a handful of amusing stories about
her
life with Franklin D. Roosevelt in this two-
disk documentary package. The former first lady
is
quite engaging as she
discusses the
first 100
days
in
office, the time
she
first met FDR,
the
assassination attempt on her husband’s
life, and
dozens of other events. The
set
is always inter-
esting and contains a
lovely picture
catalog on
the inside
flaps.
THE VOCAL STYLE OF AL MORGAN—Coral
CRL 57462/CRL 757462
The
keyboard
capabilities
of A1 Morgan
are
evident in this album, but are subordinated to the
artist’s
vocal
talents.
Spotlighting
his warmly
nostalgic handling of a dozen chestnuts, Morgan
spins a
spell for the
oldsters on tunes
like
“Is
It True What They Say About Dixie?,” “Some-
day Sweetheart” and
his way back hit “Jealous
Eyes.” The tunester
is
in
fine
fettle on
this
al-
bum which will delight many of the singer’s fans,
and sentimental listeners.
SERMON “A BAD MIND”—Rev. W. E. Hamilton
—Nashboro 10-A
Under the preaching of Rev. W.
E. Hamilton
over three thousand have been converted, and this
Nashboro recording of one of his finest practical
sermons shows the powerful emotional and logi-
cal development utilized by this splendid speaker.
The message of the founder and pastor of Hamil-
ton’s
Tabernacle
Primitive
Baptist
Church
in
Nashville
is
excitingly presented with an
intro-
duction featuring a lament-chant, and responsive
chanting by the members of the congregation.

ELLINGTON
’66 — Duke
Ellington — Reprise
R/RS-6154
A short while ago Duke Ellington came up with
a swinging jazz handling of pop tunes culled from
the best seller
lists, and the Ellington ork turns
the
trick
again with
“Ellington
’66” which
in-
cludes numbers from
the
song books
of
enter-
tainers
as
varied
as Barbra
Streisand and
the
Beatles. R&r fans might get a kick out
of the
funky
handling
of
“The
Days
Of
Wine
And
Roses” or “All My Loving,” but basically this
is
a package
for the
jazz
fiend and big band
ad-
mirer. Groovy set with plenty of spins
in store.
CANNONBALL AND COLTRANE—Cannonball
Adderley and John
Coltrane—Limelight LM/LS
86009
Heading up a tremendous Limelight release
is
this
re-issue
of an LP
cut
six years
ago
with
both John Coltrane and Julian “Cannonball” Ad-
derley appearing together. The two
saxists who
have
led
the
jazz
scene
for
several
years
play
together adeptly, and each spurs the other on to
some brilliant heights. The original album, “The
Cannonball
Adderley
Quintet
In
Chicago,”
has
not been
available for some time; but listening
to tracks like “You’re A Weaver Of Dreams” and
“Stars
Fell On Alabama” one can
be
thankful
that the album was re-released. Great
set.
THE LEE MORGAN QUINTET—Vee-Jay
2508
Enjoying
the
taste
of
success
with
his
Blue
Note outing “The Sidewinder,” Lee Morgan will
find plenty of new fans flocking to get copies of
this
set cut during his days with Vee-Jay. The
hornman
is
joined on
this waxing by some top
figures on the scene: Art Blakey, Paul Chambers
and Wynton Kelly among others. A generally soft
tone
keynotes
the
session,
which,
despite
the
“cool”
sound,
never
becomes
dull
listening.
“Bess,” and “Easy Living” top the tracks.
JAZZ BEST BETS
r-i==
MIDNIGHT PIANO—Billy Taylor—Capitol T/ST
2302
Brilliant keyboard antics from Billy Taylor are
highlighted
in
this
Capitol
set
against
three
varied backdrops of lush strings, horns and a big
band. The creative genius of Taylor and his trio,
which also includes Ben Tucker (bass) and Grady
Tate
(drums),
shimmer
in
cuts
like “My
Ro-
mance” and “You Came A Long Way From
St.
Louis.” The jazz and
college following that the
crew has accumulated will turn out in force for
this lovely
set.
THE SWINGER FROM RIO—Sergio Mendes—
Atlantic 1434
Since the original influx of Brazil’s musical ex-
ports began
to take hold
in
this country a few
years ago, larger and larger audiences began to
take
notice
of
Brazilian
Pop
Music,
or
bossa
nova. An
exciting exponent
of
this
Latin
jazz
beat,
Sergio Mendes, teams up on
this package
with one of the forefathers of bossa nova, Anto-
nio Carlos Jobim, for a captivating collection of
swingers,
including the well-known Jobim com-
positions, “The
Girl From Ipanema” and “Sam-
binha Bossa Nova.” Jazz
buffs
should
dig
this.
CLASSICAL PICKS
TWO
TWENTIETH
CENTURY
MASTER-
PIECES, BARBER-HINDEMITH VIOLIN CON-
CERTOS; Isaac Stern with the New York Phil-
harmonic
conducted
by
Leonard
Bernstein
;
Columbia ML 6113/MS 6713
Two masters unite
their powers on a
pair
of
stunning works
in
this Columbia
offering
aptly
titled
“Two
Twentieth
Century
Masterpieces.”
Leonard
Bernstein,
noted
for
his
handling
of
modern composers,
is at the peak of his pow^ers
in the conduction of the violin concertos of Sam-
uel Barber and Paul Hindemith. Likewise a vir-
tuoso, Isaac Stern
is magnificent. The works are
among the more conservative contemporary com-
positions,
and
should
be welcomed by
classical
followers
despite their modernity.
WAGNER: PARSIFAL;
Bayreuth
Festival
Re-
cording;
Philips PHM 5-550/PHS
5-950
Very few
operatic packages
require
as many
adjectives
of grandeur as
this
Philips recording
of “Parsifal.” The work
is
of such
stature;
the
task of taping the opus at a performance
in the
Bayreuth Festival
is of such magnitude; and the
cast is made up of such accomplished artists that
the set cannot but succeed in whetting the appe-
tite
of Wagnerian
discophiles. Hans
Knapperts-
busch
leads
the
orchestra
through
a
brilliant
reading behind
stellar showings by George Lon-
don, Jess Thomas and others.

JAZZ PICKS
TAKE FIVE—Carmen McRae & Dave Brubeck
Columbia CL 2316/CS 9116
Two of the jazz scene’s well-known performers,
Carmen McRae and Dave Brubeck, have teamed
up for a lively list of swinging grooves, recorded
“live” at Basin Street East in New York. Backed
by the inimitable jazz arrangements of the vet-
eran Brubeck and his refreshing keyboard
style,
the lark vocalizes her dramatic interpretations of
tunes penned by
the
pianist,
including
“It’s A
Raggy Waltz” and “In Your Own Sweet Way.”
This one
should score big with jazz
aficionados.
HUSTLIN’—Stanley Turrentine—Blue Note 4162
Stanley Turrentine and Shirley Scott head up
a top-name combo with Kenny Burrell on guitar.
Bob Cranshaw
at
bass
and
Otis
Finch
at
the
drums on this Blue Note outing, which
is
likely
to
find
a
big r&b
response
in
addition
to
the
jazzophile turn-out for the fine sounds put down.
Scott’s organ work
is brilliant on “Trouble
(No.
2)” as
is Turrentine’s sax playing. Other stand-
out
tracks
include
a “Work
Song”—like
“The
Hustler” and
“Coin’ Home,” based on Dvorak’s
5th Symphony. Excellent bluesy fare.
JAMBO
CARIBE—Dizzy
Gillespie—Limelight
LM/LS 86007
The
eye-catching
art work
on
the
covers
of
Limelight’s albums
is
spectacularly matched by
the
quality of the content within, as proved by
this Dizzy
Gillespie
offering which
is an
inter-
esting
blend
of
pure
jazz
with
a
flavoring
of
calypso. The great trumpeter
is joined by some
fine side-men, including James Moody and Kenny
Barron
in
this
session which moves from track
one
all the way through. “Fiesta Mo-Jo”
is ex-
ceptionally grand, and other highlight tracks are
“Poor Joe” and “Jambo,” both
including
vocals
by the hornman.

=

of the

MORE BLUES AND THE ABSTRACT TRUTH
—Oliver Nelson—Impulse! A/AS-75
One of the fastest rising men in the composer-
arranger jazz
field
is Oliver Nelson, who proves
his prowess with
this Impulse album which
fol-
lows
up
his
earlier
“Blues And
The
Abstract
Truth”
set. The
series
of mid and mainstream
selections are played with an exciting
liveliness
and
extreme
rapport
between
the
top-drawer
members
of
the
group.
The
title
tune, “More
Blues And The Abstract Truth,”
is a powerful
piece, followed with a great track tabbed “Blues
O’Mighty.” A grand outing.
JAZZ
ORIENT-ED—Eddie
Bonemere—Prestige
7354
The soft jazz touch of the orient is beautifully
mated with a lilting Latin beat in this easy-going
package
of sounds from Eddie Bonnemere. The
pianist
turns
out
some
lovely
listening
tracks
with Moncel on conga and bongoes, Kenny Bur-
rell
at
guitar,
Joe
Scott
on
bass,
and
George
Brown on the drums. Exquisite taste
is displayed
in the combination of eastern and western sounds,
which blend into a wonderful album. Jazz lovers,
interested in a change of pace will enjoy “Lotus
Land,” “Mr. Lucky,” and “When I Fall In Love.”
CLASSICAL PICKS
MOZART: VIOLIN CONCERTO NO.
7
IN E
FLAT, CONCERTONE IN C; Yehudi Menuhin;
Angel S 36240
Two
compositions which
have
attracted
only
minor attention
in the canon of Mozart’s works
are highlighted by outstanding readings
in
this
new Angel album featuring Yehudi Menuhin with
the Bach Festival Orchestra under the
direction
of Robert Masters. The Violin Concerto is adeptly
handled by
soloist Menuhin and
the
entire
en-
semble; and the Concertone, an outgrowth of the
“concerto grosso,” enables several other perfonn-
ers to bask in the spotlight with their solo show-
ings. An exquisite sampling.
GREAT MUSIC FOR RELAXATION—Various
Artists—RCA Victor LM/LSC-2800
Five of the finest conductors on the RCA Victor
roster have been gathered together, each leading
his own ensemble in a recording of ten selections
for
restful
listening
pleasure.
Arthur
Fiedler,
Morton Gould, Charles Munch, Leopold Stokowski
and Raymond Agoult
are
the
leaders
in works
which
include
Beethoven’s
“Moonlight
Sonata,”
and
Tchaikovski’s
“Andante
Cantabile.”
The
soothing
strains provide
excellent fare
for
late
night disk jockies and many pop music fans, and
should
see considerable
sales
activity.

CBS Reaps French Awards
NEW YORK—The Academic Charles
Cros of France has presented awards
for CBS recordings by Rudolf Serkin
and Eugene Ormandy, Mildred Miller
and Bruno Walter, Charlie Christian
and
the Benny Goodman
Orchestra,
and French artist, Barbara.
The
academy, composed
of
princi-
pal French
critics and musicologists,
annually awards prizes for the
best
recordings
in
every
field
of
music.
This year, the prize-giving ceremony
was
held
at
the
Palais
d’Orsay
in
Paris on Mar. 11.
The
Grand
Prix
for
soloists
and
Orchestra was awarded for Brahms’
“Concerto
No.
1
in
D
Minor
for
Piano and Orchestra as Op. 15,” per-
formed by
Rudolf
Serkin under the
baton
of Eugene Ormandy, and
for
Brahms’ “Alto Rhapsody, Op. 53” and
“Song of Destiny, Op. 54,” as well as
Mahler’s “Songs of a Wayfarer” in a
recording by Mezzo-Soprano Mildred
Miller and the
late conductor Bruno
Walter. The prix Reedition was pre-
sented
for
“Charlie
Christian
with
Benny Goodman,” and the Prix Paul
Gilson for “Le Temps des Lilas,” by
Barbara.

Columbia Artists To Tour Russia
Columbia
Masterworks
artists,
Isaac
Stern,
George
Sezll
and
the
Cleveland Orchestra, Eugene Istomin
and
Philippe Entremont have
sched-
uled
independent Russian
tours
this
spring.
World-famous violinist Isaac Stern,
who
is being
saluted
this month by
Columbia with the
release
of
five
of
his albums, arrives in Russia on Apr.
26,
and
his
four-week
itinerary
in-
cludes
both
recital and
concert
per-
formances
in Moscow,
Tbilisi,
Yere-
van, Riga and Tallinn.
Under the auspices of the Cultural
Presentations
Program
of
the
U.S.
State
Department, George
Szell and
the Cleveland Orchestra leave on Apr.
13 for a 24-concert tour of the Soviet
Union and Western
Europe.
Follow-
ing
five weeks in Russia, the longest
tour ever undertaken by an American
orchestra in the USSR, the group will
join
pianist Leon
Fleisher
in
Stock-
holm on May 25. Fleisher will accom-
pany them on the remainder of their
tour, which winds up
in London
on
June 26.
Eugene
Istomin, considered one
of
the
greatest
American-born
and
-trained pianists, arrived in Russia on
Apr.
5. Following a concert in Mos-
cow on Apr.
7, he will journey to Kiev
for a recital on Apr. 11 and a concert
two
days
later.
Appearances
in
Minsk, Riga and Leningrad
are
also
included in his Russian itinerary.
Philippe Entremont,
hailed on
five
continents as one
of the major pian-
ists of our day, commences his second
Russian tour on Apr.
19. Ending on
May
17, the tour includes recital and
in-concert
performances
in
Moscow
and Leningrad. The French-born pian-
ists has just completed a tour of the
United
States
and
returns
here
in
July following his Russian tour and a
visit to his native land.

Ormandy To Receive
Honorary Doctorate
NEW YORK—Eugene Ormandy, cele-
brated conductor of the
Philadelphia
Orchestra,
will
receive
an
honorary
doctorate,
the
degree
of
Doctor
of
Humane
Letters,
from Long
Island
University on Apr. 21. The presenta-
tion
will be made by
Dr.
R. Gordon
Hoxie, chancellor of Long Island Uni-
versity,
at the convocation and
dedi-
cation ceremonies
to be
held
on
the
campus
of
C.
W.
Post
College
in
Brookville, New York.
During his 29 years as music direc-
tor
of
the
Philadelphia
Orchestra,
Maestro Ormandy has received honor-
ary
doctorates
from
many
institu-
tions
including
the
University
of
Pennsylvania,
Curtis
Institute
of
Music,
Temple
University,
the
Uni-
versity
of
Michigan, Lehigh
Univer-
sity,
Clark
University
and
Rutgers
University.
Last
August,
the
conductor
and
orchestra presented a series of seven
concerts
at
C.
W.
Post
College
in
conjunction
with
the
1964
Long
Island
Festival.
April-Blackwood Grabs
Rights On British Tune
NEW YORK—Sub-publishing
rights
in the U.
S. and Canada for the Brit-
ish
smash,
“For Your
Love”,
have
been
acquired
by
April-Blackwood
Music Publishing Companies, Colum-
bia Records wholly-owned
subsidiary.
The
tune,
written
by
Graham
Gouldman,
is published in the United
Kingdom
by
Hermusic,
Ltd.,
and
rights
for
the
American
firm
were
acquired by Nat Shapiro,
director
of
Columbia’s
international
publishing
operations.
The hot English
disk, scheduled to
be
released
in
the
States
on
Epic,
was recorded by
the
Yardbirds, who
are
currently appearing
at London’s
Craw Daddy Club.

Mercury Rushes New
Freddie & Dreamers Deck
CHICAGO—^Not
even
the
Atlantic
ocean
stops
a
rush-rush
singles
re-
lease
these
days.
Mercury
Records
initiated
a
jet-age
release
of
a new
Freddie & The Dreamers
single
last
week, an
item, “Do The
Freddie.” A
special
lyric was penned
in
Chicago
and last Monday
(5), Lou Reizner, of
Mercury’s
import
division,
flew
the
item
to
Manchester,
England, where
it was cut the following day. By the
middle
of the week, the tape was
at
Mercury’s
Richmond,
Va.
pressing
plant. The deck was
set
to be
in the
hands of retailers
last weekend.
Harry Miller Visits U.S.
NEW YORK—Harry Miller, the Aus-
tralian and New Zealand music man,
visited
the
U.
S.
last week
to
con-
clude some deals. Arriving from a 10
day visit from England and the Con-
tinent, Miller said he renewed repre-
sentation agreements with the Cameo-
Parkway and Roulette labels for New
Zealand’s
La
Gloria
label.
Miller
is
foreign
rep for the
label. Two years
ago
he
sold 80%
of
his
interest
in
the label, retaining a 20%
share.
Miller
also books
acts for Austra-
lia and New
Zealand. One upcoming
project
is a “South
Pacific Folk Fes-
tival”
featuring
Judy
Collins,
Josh
White
and Bud &
Travis.
Package
will play Australia and New Zealand
beginning May
19.
Before returning
to
his home base
in Australia, Miller planned a stay of
several days on the west coast.

the

to mark the observance

1-10.

COOLIDGE KUDOS—Dudley H. Toller-Bond, executive vice president of Lon-
don
Records,
congratulates
his
label’s
composer-pianist
Mrs.
Peggy
Stuart
Coolidge aboard the Queen Mary when she sailed for Russia and Poland as the
first American woman composer to have been
officially invited to perform her
works and meet
in symposia with outstanding composers
in
those
countries.
They are holding the flag of the U.S. which had been flown over the Capitol in
recognition of her accomplishments
in furthering the cause
of better under-
standing among nations through the universal language of music.
Looking on are J. R. Coolidge, and Mrs. Toller-Bond.

By Belford Hendricks
NEW
YORK — Arranger - composer
Belford
Hendricks
has
set
up
his
own production company
called
Con-
clave
Record
Corp.
He has
signed pianist Alan Logan
and
the
first
production
is
an
in-
strumental
titled
“Twilight”
backed
with “What Now My
Love.”
Hend-
ricks
expects
to have
the
first
disk
placed with
a
label
in
the next few
days.
He
is
currently
rounding
up
vocal talent and songs for future pro-
ductions.
Hendricks
will
still
do
free
lance
arranging for various companies.
The vet arranger started his musi-
cal
career
in
Terre
Haute,
Indiana
where
he
attended
Ir diana
State
Teachers
College.
After
graduation,
he played with many Mid-west bands
and
finally started doing a
single. In
1949
he
moved
to New
York
and
resumed
his musical
studies
at New
York
University.
After
completing
his studies
there, he went into
song-
writing,
co-composing
such
hits
as
“Looking
Back,”
“Nothing
In
The
World,”
“Call Me” and
“It’s Just A
Matter
Of
Time.”
Hendricks
then
went
into
arranging,
doing most
of
the
Dinah
Washington’s
and
Brook
Benton’s biggest hits including “What
A Difference A Day Made” for Dinah
and
“Boll Weevil” for Benton. Other
hits
include Timi Yuro’s “Hurt,” A1
Martino’s
“I
Love
You
Because,”
Phyllis McGuire’s “I Don’t Want To
Walk Without You,” Aretha Frank-
lins “Runnin’ Out Of Fools” and Nat
Cole’s “Ramblin’
Rose.”

Sam Fox Music Mores
Into Show Music Area
NEW YORK—Fred Fox, president of
the
Sam
Fox
Publishing
Company,
has
set up a production unit for the
musical show field.
As a partner in his producing team,
Fred Fox has secured the services of
Robert M. Lewis, who has been asso-
ciated with Broadway productions in
various
capacities
for many
years.
Fox has entered into Dramatics’ Guild
contracts with, and has signed on a
long
term
basis,
several
teams
of
show writers for the development
of
Broadway properties.
It
is
Fox’s
contention
that music
publishers can make major
contribu-
tions
to the
quality of contemporary
musical
theater,
enabling
such
pub-
lishers
to control the musical aspects
involving
both
the
production
itself
as well as the negotiations with major
record companies for the release and
exploitation of original cast albums.
As
an
initial
production. Fox has
acquired the publishing rights to the
new musical by Ray Golden, “What
This Country Needs,” which opens at
the Music Box Theater in Hollywood
on
July
14
and
then
in New York
later in the fall.
In the weeks ahead, Fox will make
additional
announcements
of
specific
projects as they come to fruition.

Decca/London's Culshaw
Makes Brief U.S. Visit
NEW YORK—John
Culshaw,
pro-
ducer
of
classical
projects
for
the
London
label, made
a
short
visit
to
New York last week, his first trek to
these shores in nine years.
Two-fold purpose
of
his
visit was
to
introduce
him
to
London
execs
here and promote his latest recording
date,
a new
version
of
“Gotterdam-
merung.”
The
stellar
east
includes
Birgit
Nielssen,
Gottlob
Frick,
Die-
trich
Fischer-Dieskau,
Christa
Lud-
wig and Georg
Solte conducting the
Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra.
JOHN CULSHAW
The trade press was invited to hear
portions of the work, part of London’s
June release, at a reception last Mon-
day at the Essex House, this city.
In the past 10 years, Culshaw has
produced a number
of important
re-
leases
for London, American
affiliate
of
British
Decca,
including
the
first
version
of
Britten’s
prize-winning
“War
Requiem.”
Others
include
“Rheingold,”
“Tristan
und
Isolde,”
“Aida,”
“Salome,”
and
“Siegfried.”
Culshaw,
now
back
in
England,
joined Decca/London
in
1946
at
the
age of 22.
In
1959, he
and
his Vienna crew
(all
from
England)
were
awarded
the
Nicolai
Medal
by
the
Vienna
Philharmonic,
an
honor
previously
reserved for composers or performing
artists.
Economides
Forms
Production
Firm
HOLLYWOOD—Jim Economides, for-
mer A&R man with Capitol Records,
has
started
his own production firm
with
offices
located
at
9122
Sunset
Blvd. in Los Angeles.
Economides,
who
left
Capitol
in
March
after two
years
as
producer
for Bobby Darin, Jack Lemmon, Dick
Dale
and
The
Lettermen,
among
others, was responsible for more than
20 national chart albums.
The new production
firm. Gauntlet
Productions
Ltd., will serve both the
recording
and
television
industries
and can
fill the void for, what Econo-
mides terms, is a “desperate need for
small reliable, independent production
companies.” Economides believes that
A and R men have become too expen-
sive for small companies to carry on
a
staff
basis and many independent
producers
are far from
reliable. He
intends to offer a complete production
job on singles, albums and specialized
industrial
tapes.
At Capitol Economides was also in-
volved
in
the preparation
of
special
“Hot Rod” and “Surf” programs and
will offer this experience to prospec-
tive
clients. Deals have already been
set
with
United
Artists Music
Inc.
and Seeburg Music Libraries. Econo-
mides has been
in the recording
in-
dustry for the past nine years
and,
prior
to
joining
Capitol, was
a top
recording
engineer
with
United
Re-
cording Company in Holljnvood.

NAACP Award To
Florence Greenberg
NEW YORK—Florence
Greenberg,
president of Scepter Records, has been
presented an award by the
Passaic,
N.J. chapter of the NAACP for her
“continuing
and
untiring
efforts
in
music on behalf of her stars.”
At a
special ceremony on Sunday,
April 25, her son, Stanley Greenberg,
was given
the award on her behalf.
She has been on vacation for the past
five weeks.
It was
pointed
out
that
she
has
been
a constant force
in many
civic
organizations
as
well
as
a
valued
participant
in
the
civil
rights move-

Original Victor Art
Displayed In Chicago
CHICAGO—RCA Victor Records
dis-
played some of the prize winning
al-
bum
cover
art
that has
embellished
the
label’s product for the past
sev-
eral years at an Exhibition
of Origi-
nal Album
Cover Art
last Saturday
(1)
on
the
second
floor
at Lyon &
Healy
Company
in
this
city.
Lyon
& Healy tied this program in with the
celebration
of National Music Week.
Supervising the program for Lyon &
Healy
was
Robert
Storm,
advertis-
ing
manager.
This
novel
idea was
first
initiated
by Ralph Ergas, manager of the disk
division of RCA Dist. in Des Plaines,
111., several months ago. He then sub-
mitted
it to George Marek, vice pres,
and general manager of RCA Victor
Records.
Ergas explained that this exhibition
contains the work of some of Ameri-
ca’s most widely known and
success-
ful
artists. Some
of them have had
works
exhibited
in major museums,
foremost
art
galleries,
and
colleges
in
the
U.S.A.
Several
of the
artists
have works
in the permanent
collec-
tions
of
the
Whitney
Museum,
the
Museum
of Modern
Art,
the
Metro-
politan Museum, the Library of Con-
gress,
the
Cincinnati
Museum,
the
Dallas Museum, and others.
All the works to be shown are the
result
of
direct
commissions
to
the
artists by Victor. In most
cases, the
artists were directed only
to
the
ex-
tent that they were
to
interpret the
particular work of a composer. None
of the works are for
sale.
Some
26
works
of
art
are
being
exhibited, ranging from
oil canvasses
to
collages,
and
pen
drawings,
etc.
Among the noted
artists represented
are:
Lawrence
Beall
Smith,
Mario
Leone,
Joe
Lombardaro,
Richard
M.
Powers, Eugene Karlin, Federico Cas-
tellon,
Richard Dodge,
A.
Zakanych,
Joseph Hirsch, Mike Ludlow, A. Pow-
ell, Jan
Balet, Eugene Berman, Mo-
zelle
Thompson,
Boris
Artzybasheff,
Herschel Levit, William Ward Beech-
er, and Victor Kalin.
Ergas
stated,
in
conclusion,
that
this
is the very first time such an ex-
hibition of album cover art had been
held at any
retail music firm
in
this
area. Lyon & Healy highlighted
this
occasion
with
a
large
window
dis-
play, and signs throughout the
store
that
pointed
up
to
the
location
in
the
building where
the
exhibit was
being
held.

MPM Goes On Latin Tour
In spite of the early hour the airport in Sao Paulo was crowded for a warm
farewell to Brazil’s most representative artists of the moment who are going
for a tour in Lima, Peru, and probably
other Latinamerican
countries. The
Zimbo Trio and Elis Regina are on their way to what will most likely be the
beginning of a snowballing new promotion of the Modern Popular Music
of
Brazil in the outside. Besides the many fans of the lark and of the combo, we
could see Enrique Lebendiger, prexy of Fermata and of Discos RGE; Mario
Duarte, representing Companhia Brasileira De
Discos
(Philips)
and
several
other people connected with the music world, the press, radio and TV.
Speaking of Elis Regina, the songstress was inked by TV-Record, Channel 7
of Sao Paulo, for a six month period, for TV and theater shows, with one of
the best paid contracts lately.
The new Zimbo Trio album was
finished just before the departure
of the
three musicians and
it is even better than the
first one. In the meantime, the
U.S. tour of the group is being planned and there are already several people
interested in them.

*Indicates Local Product.
Max Gold, who acts as PR man for the Todamerica pubbery
is very happy
with the international success of the Brazilian number “Deixa Isso P’ra La,”
which Sao Paulo “sambista” Jair Rodrigues made famous through his hand-
movement interpretation
(it was for several weeks on the Best
Sellers’
list).
Connie Francis, two days after her return to the U.S., was sending an advance-
ment for the publishing of the number
in the
U.S., which
she was already
actively learning during her recent stay
in Brazil. Augusto Alguero, Carmen
Sevilla’s husband who, besides being a well known composer in Spain, also has
his own pubbery in Madrid, also sent advancement for the publishing of that
song, which will probably be cut by his wife, with Spanish lyrics. The tune was
already recorded in Argentina by Los Dukes in twist rhythm. Another number
by the same authors, also sung by Rodrigues is “Zigue-Zague,” which tries the
same approach.
There was a very successful cocktail-party hosted by Discos Farroupilha for
the official launching of the third album by Pedrinho Mattar Trio, which is even
better than the other two. The Zimbo Trio, who was also present, played with
the Mattar Trio and all the people present heard some excellent music. Among
the crowd we could see Ramalho Neto and Mojica of RCA Victor, which
is in
charge of the promotion and distribution of the Farroupilha label, as well as
three
girls who received third prize at the
“I Festival of Brazilian Popular
Music,” Vera
Brasil, Miriam
Ribeiro,
composers
and
Claudete
Soares,
tiny
songstress.
Other
guests
included composer Adilson
Godoy,
musician
Saba,
songster Geraldo Vandre, new RGE manager Julio Nagib, and representatives
of press, radio and TV. Incidentally, Farroupilha is proud of its latest releases
which are a good beginning for a young company. Among these are “0 Que
Cantamos na TV,” a
selection of the ihost
successful numbers
of the
vocal
group. Os Farroupilhas, “Tema do Boneco de Palha,” by Vera Brasil, “0 As-
sunto
.
.
. Edgard” with guitarist Antonio Edgard Gianullo in a good selec-
tion
of BNN numbers, and “12 x Bossa Nova,” with numbers by Os
Far-
roupilhas, Pedrinho Mattar Trio, Edgard and Vera Brasil. There
is also a teen-
music release by a new group called the Lions, which
is starting to
sell well.
The three young men and two larks who make up the Farroupilhas are also
preparing a tour in Latinamerica and will then produce a show with themselves,
the Jongo Trio and a new songstress not yet revealed. It would also be a good
show to present in the USA!
Today we have some news from CBS do Brasil. The
title of the new LP by
Abdias
is “Tarrabufado” and the
label
is expecting the same
success as
its
predecessors. Astor Silva is again collaborating with Sidney on the new album
of the series “Isto
£: Danga.” Carlos Alberto is choosing repertoire for his 4th.
album, while Carlos Jose
is having another hit with his rendition of “Queria,”
which
is one of the bands in the album “As 14 Mais, Vol. XV.” A new artist
Eduardo Costa and his Group, is finishing his first LP for the CBS label, with
a good
selection
of MPM numbers. Newcomers pacted by the company
are
songsters Ricardo Lopes and Genaro Pacheco and a hammond-organ
player
called
Lafayette. Young
teen
idol
Roberto
Carlos
has
another
hit
on
the
market, “Historia De Um Homem Mau.”
The textile firm Rhodiaceta, who co-sponsored the “I National
Festival
of
Brazilian Popular Music” is definitely one of the good promoters of the MPM.
Livio Rangan, who is in charge of the publicity for the company, is preparing
a European tour (Portugal, Spain, France and Italy) and will probably come
to the US later with a musical-fashion show featuring Wilson Simonal, Marly
Tavares, the Bossa 3 and probably some “passistas” and one more singer, not
yet chosen. Also under preparation is a sort of new Festival, with high awards
to newcomers, and a special presentation of the biggest names in the Modern
Music world. It will be called the “Bossa Nova Nova” Festival and will give a
chance for new names to appear and will be held during the Annual Textile
Fair,
“Fenit”.
Arrangements
are
being made
for
the
organization
of
the
Second Festival of Brazilian Popular Music, for next year, which this time,
thankfully, will be handled by different producers.
Ramalho Neto, promo general manager of RCA Victor in Sao Paulo, told us
about an important meeting held in Mexico City, the Convention of Executives
of Latin America Subsidiaries of RCA Records. This Convention was presided
over by George Marex and E.
J. Dale, and systems and
policies
to be used
during this year, were discussed. Brasil was represented by Douglas J. M. Reid,

NEW YORK—Bernard
Kalban
has
been
named
manager
of
the
Mills
Music’s
educational
department,
Waren
Ling,
vice-president and
gen-
eral manager, has announced. Kalban
replaces Don
Malin, who
left
to
as-
sume
the
educational
post
at
E.
B.
Marks Music
Corp.
With
Mills Music
since
1960,
Kal-
ban moves up
from
his
advertising-
promotion
role
there.
Prior
to
1960
he
performed
in
executive
capacity
for
Hansen
Publications,
Inc.,
also
serving
a previous
hitch
at
Mills.
At the same time, Ling named two
important
additions
to
the
Mills
Music
executive
staff
with
the
ap-
pointment
of
Samuel
Rubenstein
as
controller and Lawrence
Lighter,
at-
torney,
to
legal and
special
adminis-
trative
duties.
Lighter
moves
over
from
SESAC
where
he
performed
similar tasks. Graduate of New York
University
School
of
Law,
he
ma-
jored
in
copyright
law,
writing
a
graduate paper
on
“Record
Piracy.”
Rubenstein resigned
his position as
controller
of Peter Pan Industries
to
accept
the
present
appointment
and
will assume complete financial respon-
sibilities for the music firm. He
is an
accounting graduate
of
City
College
of New York.
All three execs will report directly
to
Ling.
These
mark
the
first
im-
portant
changes
in
Mills Music
per-
sonnel since purchase by Utilities and
Industries
Corp.
Mills
Music
Trust
units are now being traded
over-the-
counter.

JAZZ PICKS
YOU BETTER BELIEVE ME—Ramsey
Lewis
Trio and Jean DuShon—Argo 750
The
brilliance of Ramsey Lewis’ Trio
is linked
with
the
fiery
vocal
talents
of Jean DuShon
in
this Argo outing. Departing from the trio’s usual
format, there
is also an added threesome on flute,
guitar and sax on the first side of the LP. These
combinations give
startling new
shadings
to
the
sound of each
in a
set that should garner plenty
of
spins. Among the
fine sounds
are: “Who Can
I Turn
To,” “Let
It Be Me” and “My
Coloring
Book.”
FUCHSIA
SWING
SONG—Sam
Rivers—Blue
Note 4184
Some like
it hot, and this
is a set to
suit them.
Sam
Rivers wails
in top form on
this
collection
of six self-penned tunes, with fine accompaniment
afforded by Jaki Byrd (piano), Ron Carter (bass)
and
Anthony
Williams
(drums).
The
swinging
sounds
of
the
tenor
saxist show
a
vigor tinged
with
blues
through
this
Blue
Note
recording;
with
outstandingly
distinctive
tracks
including
“Fuchsia Swing Song,” Cyclic Episode” and “Lu-
minous Monolith.” Should
sell very well.
JAZZ BEST BETS
I TALK WITH THE SPIRITS—Roland Kirk-
Limelight LM/LS
86008
Prize packages seem to have become a habit at
Limelight, where the jackets are as delightful to
behold
as
the
records
are
to
listen
to.
Roland
Kirk’s outing, tabbed after one
of the tracks,
“I
Talk With The Spirits,” is no exception. The flau-
tist shows up wonderfully with
able accompani-
ment from
Horace
Parian
on
piano,
and
some
strong sounds from
the
rest of the
sidemen. In-
cluded among the
fine
tracks are “Django”
and
“A Quote From
Clifford Brown.”
THE VOICE THAT IS!—Johnny Hartman—Im-
pulse A/AS-74
Johnny Hartman goes
all out on
this
set with
Latin percussion backing and a dozen tunes with
a
widely
varied
appeal.
The
smooth
songster’s
lush
voice
imparts
a warmth
that
at
once
ca-
resses
and
enlivens
each
of
the
tunes
with
a
freshness that should make this LP a choice ad-
dition
to many
collections. Easy
going
stylings
and velvet renditions on
this Bob Thiele produc-
tion include: “Joey, Joey, Joey” from “The Most
Happy Fella” and “It Never Entered My Mind.”
An impressive outing.
HIP CAKE WALK—Don
Patterson &
Booker
Ervin—Prestige
7349
A lot of swing, some great talent and tremen-
dous
effort have gone
into
this
Prestige
outing,
and the results are
terrific. The wild combination
of Don Patterson at the organ and Booker Ervin
on
tenor
sax makes
for
top drawer moving on
up-tempo
tracks
like
“Rosetta”
and
“Sister
Ruth,” with more sedate though
decidedly
lively
grooving
in
store on both tracks on the B
side.
Blues fans will get as big a kick out of this LP
as
the
jazz
buffs who
should
really
enjoy
the
workouts
here.

Tape Association (MRIA)
Merges With EIA
WASHINGTON—The
Magnetic
Re-
cording Industry Association and the
Electronic
Industries
Association
have agreed
to merge
under
a
plan
adopted by members
of both associa-
tions.
Approval
of
the merger
plan was
announced jointly last week by W. G.
Paradis, MRIA
president, and James
D.
Secrest, EIA executive
vice
presi-
dent,
following
a
proxy
meeting
of
EIA
members. MRIA
members
had
previously approved the proposal fol-
lowing
affirmative
action
by
both
boards
of
directors.
Paradis
is
vice
president and general manager of the
radio
products
division
of Warwick
Electronics
Inc.,
Chicago.
“We
believe
this
merger
will
be
beneficial
to members
of both associ-
ations
and
will
enable
EIA
to
strengthen
its
representation
in
an
important
sector
of
the
electronics
industry,”
Paradis
and
Secrest
said
in a joint statement.
“The
combined
organization
will
operate under
the name
of EIA
be-
cause of
its comprehensive character,
representing
manufacturers
of
all
electronic
products.
However, mem-
bers
of MRIA
will have a
‘home’
in
EIA which will adapt its organization
and services to meet the requirements
of the producers of magnetic record-
ing equipments and components.”
A
conference
of
former
MRIA
members,
including
those who
have
been EIA members as well, has been
scheduled on May 26
at the O’Hare
Inn
in
Chicago.
“The purpose of this meeting,” Sec-
rest explained, “is to let MRIA mem-
bers get acquainted with EIA and to
let EIA
officers
and
staff members
know what
is expected
of EIA
as
a
result
of the
merger.”
MRIA was formed
in 1952
in New
York
City.
It
later moved
its
head-
quarters
to
Chicago.
MRIA had more than 30 members
of which eight have also belonged to
EIA. Most
of the new members
will
be
assigned
either
to
the
consumer
products
division
or
the
Parts
Divi-
sion. The
latter
already has
several
sections
operating
in
the
magnetic
components
area.
The
MRIA-EIA
merger
will
be-
come effective on issuance of a certif-
icate by the state of Illinois in which
both
associations
were
incorporated.

NEW YORK—The
Paramount
Pic-
tures
Corp.,
the
parent
firm
of Dot
Records, more than doubled
its earn-
ings in the
first quarter, according to
a report issued
last week by George
Weltner,
president
of
the
company.
Consolidated
net
profit
of
Para-
mount for the
quarter ended Apr.
3
amounted to $2,186,000, equal to $1.39
a share, on 1,569,956 shares outstand-
ing. In the same period last year the
company
earned
$1,041,000,
or
63
cents a share from operations. An ad-
ditional gain of $723,000, or 44 cents
a share, from the
sale of investment,
brought
the
net income
for
1964
to
a total of $1,764,000, or $1.07 a share.

A&L & Alsam
Distribs
Celebrate 5th Army
PHILADELPHIA—A measure of the
success
of
Philly’s A&L and Alsam
distrib outlets in its first five years
a current anniversary celebration—is
that
their
growth
has
forced
three
relocations to larger quarters.
A1 Melnick, who formed the outlets
five years ago after a
stint as a key
salesman
at Marnel
of
Philadelphia,
says
that
“coverage
and
promotion
are our
strongest
assets.” These
as-
sets
are
delivered by a
staff
of
vet
music
men.
It
includes
Del
Greene,
head
of the
sales
dept, who came to
the firm after 10 years of experience
with
Korvette, Kapp
and
S.
Klein;
promo men
Harry
Fink
and
Barry
Abrams, who have
30
years
of
disk
promo
experience
behind
them;
and
a
salesman
crew
composed
of
Jay
Freedman and Craig
Smith. Melnick
himself has
been
on
the
disk
scene
for
16 years.
When A&L first got started
it had
one shipper and one
girl
in the
office
and bookkeeping departments. There
are now
three
shippers,
headed
by
Jackie Villanueva, an
office manager
(Celia Biberman)
and her
assistant.
The firm handles a number of disk
areas,
including pop,
classical,
inter-
national, spoken word,
spiritual, folk
jazz and kiddie disks.
It also imports
transistor radios, portable TV’s, tape
recorders and Magnus Organs.
Some of the company’s major disk
lines include Amy-Mala, Audio Fidel-
ity, Elektra, Fantasy, Folkways, Spo-
ken-Arts, Tikva, among others. Home
for the distrib is 1811 Fairmount Ave.

the
Bachelors
visited
the
U.
S.
re-
cently
for
a
guest
shot
on
the Ed
Sullivan Show and
to
do some
pro-
motional carousing at a cocktail party
held
in
their honor by London Rec-
ords. The threesome is shown (top to
bottom) meeting WMCA “Good Guy”
Joe O’Brien; diskery exec Herb Gold-
farb and Dorothy Solomon, their man-
ager;
CB
general
manager
Marty
Ostrow;
and
“Hullabaloo”
producer
Gary Smith. The fruits of their labor
may be seen in a rapidly rising chart
item, “Marie.”

SWEDEN
The copyright dispute continues as far as the song “Cadillac”
is concerned.
Originally recorded by the British group The Renegades for Scandiain Finland,
Scandia-Musiikki Oy claimed that it was the original publisher. Sweden Music
AB became the Swedish publisher, and the song was recorded by the Hep Stars
for Olga in Sweden. At this time, Belinda in London claimed it was their song.
When on the charts in Sweden, the song was listed in Cash Box with the name
of both these publishers. However, now
it
is claimed that “Cadillac”
is Chuck
Berry’s, “No Money Down” from Arch Music Corp. in New York, published in
Sweden by the newly founded American Songs AB, headed by Felix Stahl.
In
Stockholm
for three days
last week was Miguel Smirnoff
of Cash
Box,
Argentina. Arriving here from Germany, he spent a couple of days in Copen-
hagen before coming here and ended
his Scandinavian
visit with
a couple
of
days among the Norwegian
Fjords.
Another South American visitor, also in town, was Luis A. Aubry of Indus-
trial
Sono-Radio. Lima, Peru. Attending the IFPI
Council
Meeting,
this was
his first visit to Stockholm. Aubry told Cash Box that, in Peru, the importance
of domestic music
is most
notable. No matter how good
it might
be
for
a
Peruvian company to get the representation of one or two foreign labels,
if
it
has no domestic record label, the company might find
it
difficult to exist. And,
according to Aubry, this
is not only typical of Peru, but of the whole
of the
South American market.

releases from Cupol

on Dot, Birthe Wilke on Triola with a Swedish version of “Hush, Hush, Sweet

copyrights,

City by the end of the year. EMI will be identified here as “Capitol de Mexico^

“Imperial do Brasil” from Rio de Janeiro, which also

(EMI). We were unofficially informed that Mario Gil also will be part of the
EMI organization in Mexico.

dynamic

in

Opening

fol-

in Eu-
rope, during which year company of-
fices were opened in Rome, Paris and

It was at that time that the

John Mather

a major

tinental

last

in Munich.
The London

is occupying his-

Handel

at
25

erick Handel.
Mather has organized a

to carry on the wide-scale mo-
tion picture, television, legitimate the-
atre, literary and dramatic
activities
of the London agency operation.
Four

ther are John Findlay, Richard East-
ham, David Booth and
Sally
Shuter.
Booth formerly was

Ltd.
Eastham has
a broad background in
legitimate
theatre. Miss
Shuter was
1 head of television casting for London
Artists, and Findlay
is a well-known
!
talent agency executive with wide ex-

Mercury Names New Canadian Distrib
CHICAGO—Mercury
Records
last
week
consumated
a
licensing
deal
which
will transfer Mercury product
in Canada from
Quality Records
of
Canada to London Records of Canada
on July
1.
The new licensee will rep
all
affili-
ated labels in the Mercury corporate
entity
(Mercury,
Philips,
Limelight,
Wing,
Cumberland,
Fontana,
Blue
Rock and Smash).
The actual mechanics of the switch
were worked out in a series of confer-
ences
between
Mercury
brass
and
London execs Fraser Jamieson, man-
aging director, Alice Koury, assistant
general manager and Gilles Albin, na-
tional sales manager.
The flow of parts and promotional
materials
was
a
major
concern
of
Mercury. These
details were worked
in a series of special confabs with the
label’s product managers.
London executives
will be working
closely
with
Mercury’s
Lou
Rienzer
who has been assigned
to assure the
simultaneous
release
of
product
in
both the U.
S. and Canada.
London
is
currently
reassigning
some of their top execs to handle the
new product. An end-of-June meet at
London’s St. Laui'ent home-office with
Mercury’s
sales
management
team
will
decide upon
last minute
details
for the
distribution set-up. Personnel
from
London’s
four
company-owned
branches and one indie distrib will be
present at the meet.

John Gary Triumphs
At The
Persian Room
NEW YORK—The nonchalant remark
made by one guest at last week’s Per-
sian Room opening of John Gary best
summarizes what the entire audience
thought about his debut performance.
He tuiTied to his wife in a taken-for-
granted tone
of voice and
said with
confidence,
“The
Persian Room
has
another star.”
The young and handsome RCA Vic-
tor vocalist has been developing beau-
tifully
as
a
performer and
his
tre-
mendous
acceptance
at
the
Persian
Room
of
the
swank
Plaza
Hotel
in
this
city
should add
further
fuel
to
the career of a rapidly rising
star.
The qualities that made Gary so ap-
pealing
to
the
opening
nighters
can
be summed up very simply: Gary has
a
great
voice, amazing
range,
sings
great songs, has the looks and
is ex-
tremely
charming.
You’re
with
him
and for him even before he sings one
note. And once he opens his pipes, you
have to fall for him.
It was also a great pleasure hearing
songs, originally designed to be sung
without a
beat, sung just
that way.
With many
ballad
singers
swinging
everything and anything to a blaring
rhythm backdrop, it was indeed a nov-
elty having
a
beautiful
voice
in
the
foreground unclouded by swinging in-
struments.
His
setting for the
classic “Danny
Boy” is brilliant as is the presentation
of the song which follows. Gary
dis-
played his power when he came on to
the stage singing the
final chorus of
“More.”
It’s a magnificent
voice. He
also
displayed
a
delightful
sense
of
humor as he traced the transition
of
“O Sole Mio.” He used the guitar dur-
ing one segment of the show for an
effective change of pace.
In
addition
to great singing and a
well paced show, Gary’s conversation
was relaxed, natural and delightfully
“un-hip.”
It won’t be long before we’ll be see-
ing Gary on the TV variety show cir-
cuit with great frequency.
It’s inevit-
able with his talent and looks.
Renee
Raff To AF
NEW YORK—Audio
Fidelity
head
Herman
D. Gimbel has just signed a
versatile young
artist
to
his
rapidly
expanding roster. She is Renee Raff, a
26 year
old
singer-pianist who heads
her own trio.
Born
in
Cape
Town,
she
took up
piano at age 7 and, after winning sev-
eral
local awards, went to London to
study
voice
at
the Royal
College
of
Music when she was
19. Upon receiv-
ing her diploma, she went straight to
work
at
the Casanova
Club,
playing
there for two years while making per-
sonal
and
television
appearances
throughout Europe.
She arrived in the United States in
1957, whereupon
she was
signed by
MCA and booked into the better New
York hotels, such as the Commodore,
Pierre,
Waldorf-Astoria,
Delmonico,
Sherry-Netherlands,
and
Carlyle.
While continuing with her career, the
artist also began studjfing progressive
jazz piano
in
1959 with John Mehe-
gan at Juuliard, with whom
she
re-
mained for two years.

Broadway musical hits, introduced here in Japan on films and on stage, are
coming on strong and booming in the record
field. Each of the record compa-
nies
is very eager
to
release
this music
either
in
original
cast
version
or
sound track. The show music records now on the market, including the jazz
and moody arrangements,
are
nearly
innumerable.
Relating
to the
original Broadway
cast
discs,
the
following
are
released
by Nippon Columbia, which was
the
first company
to
release
this
sort
of
musical and putting one on the market
last January. At
first, the
firm
re-
leased the sound track recordings which
hit big causing the
label
to release
a
series
of Broadway musicals,
in various
arrangements. They
are
“Annie,
Get Your Gun” by Doris Day, “King And I” by Barbara Cooke, “Oklahoma”
by John Layton, “Show Boat” by Barbara Cooke, as well as “South
Pacific,”
“Kiss Me, Kate” and two
others, making ten in
all.
From Teichiku Records, “Annie, Get Your Gun” and “King And
I” were
released in the April issue, and “Oklahoma” will be put on the market in June.
“A-Merry-Go-Round,” “Porgy And Bess” and “Guys And
Dolls”
are
sched-
uled from Toshiba
Records, who
released “No
Strings”
last
year. Also
re-
lating
to
the
sound
track
discs, Nippon
Victor
plans
to
release “Sound
of
Music”
in June, while Nippon Grammohon has already released “Annie, Get
Your Gun” in May and plans to release “Mary Poppins,” and Capitol released
“King And
I,” “High Society,” “A-Merry-Go-Round” and “Oklahoma,”
all of
which have become best-sellers.
In
jazz arrangements, “My Fair Lady,” by Nat King
Cole, Oscar
Peter-
son Trio and The Andre Previn Quartet are on the
scene, while “Sound Of
Music” by Edmund Ros, “Hello, Dolly” by Louis Armstrong and “West Side
Story” by Oscar Peterson Trio are
also shown.
Popular records recommended by recent Japanese pop and jazz magazines
are shown as follows:
1. “Pat
Boone/Love
Letters”
(Dot)
including “My
Prayer”
and
“Twilight
Time.”
2. “Doris Day/Musical Album”
(Columbia)
including “They Say
It’s Won-
derful” and “Do Re Mi.”
3. “Sammy Davis Junior”
(Reprise)
including “My Foolish Heart” and “Bye
Bye Blackbird.”
4. “The Best Album Of Dean Martin”
(Reprise)
including “Besame Mucho”
and “La Vie En Rose.”
5. “Connie
Francis
Sings
Latin”
(MGM)
including
“La
Malaguena”
and
“Granada.”
6. “The Sound Of Music” (Victor)
soundtrack.
7. “Cascading Strings By Mantovani” including
“I’ll Get By” and “Fly Me To
The Moon.”
8. “Carmen
Cavallero A La Mode”
(Decca)
including “September
Song.”
9. “Sam
Taylor
In Japan”
includes “Harlem

Starting in 1966, Sweden will arrange

to
